title: Canarsie Traditional Land
summary: Canarsie homelands are remembered across present-day Brooklyn, Flatlands, Jamaica, the bay islands, and western Long Island. Early Dutch and English records place Canarsie people in relation to coastal villages, waterways, neighboring Native communities, land negotiations, and continued western Long Island Native presence.
why_this_matters: Canarsie Traditional Land presents Brooklyn and western Long Island as Native homeland. The page connects place names, colonial records, Lenape-related language context, and public memory without reducing Canarsie history to a myth of disappearance.
history_title: Canarsie In Dutch And English Records
history_content: Seventeenth-century Dutch and English records preserve Canarsie-related names in grants, petitions, and patent descriptions. These records show Native land relationships being translated into colonial property systems while Canarsie people remained part of western Long Island political and cultural history. Later histories sometimes turned Canarsie into folklore or disappearance stories. The references is presented carefully here with Native presence at the center.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The western Brooklyn and western Jamaica Bay context around Canarsie and Flatlands shown west of the Rockaway wedge on the Martine reference illustration, including Floyd Bennett Field and Shirley Chisholm State Park in this broad display. The dividing lines with Rockaway and Matinecock are interpretive display boundaries, not surveyed historical borders.
